query: Meta capital expenditure guidance AI infrastructure
normalized: ai capital expenditure guidance infrastructure meta

output.content:
**Meta’s latest FY2026 capital-expenditure guidance is $130 billion–$145 billion**, inclusive of principal payments on finance leases; this is the outlook issued with Q2 results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. [[1]] 

The range was narrowed upward from **$125 billion–$145 billion** following Q1, implying a **$5 billion increase at the midpoint**, while the $145 billion upper bound was retained. [[2, 3]] 

For context, Meta initially guided to **$115 billion–$135 billion** for 2026, with year-over-year growth attributed to investment supporting Meta Superintelligence Labs and the core business. [[4]] 

Meta spent **$31.08 billion in Q2 2026** and **$19.84 billion in Q1**, with spending directed to servers, data centers, and network infrastructure. [[1, 5, 2]] 

Management’s stated uses for the AI-infrastructure build include model training, scaling the core advertising/business platform, personal agents and new products, and eventually serving large external customers; it also is laying data-center and network foundations for compute expansion in 2028 and beyond. [[2]] 

The Q1 guidance increase reflected expected higher component prices and, to a lesser extent, incremental data-center costs for future-year capacity. [[6, 3]] 

A useful scale comparison is that Meta’s FY2025 capex was **$72.22 billion**, so the current FY2026 guidance implies an approximately **80%–101% increase year over year**. [[4, 1]] 

The principal analytical takeaway is that Meta is explicitly accepting a near-term cash-flow and depreciation burden to secure AI capacity ahead of demand, rather than sizing infrastructure solely to current utilization; investors should therefore track capex execution, infrastructure-driven operating-expense growth, and evidence of monetization in ads, AI products, and enterprise offerings. [[2, 4]]
